w: Zagreb's skyline signature is this church's roof — a mosaic of coloured tiles laying out the coats of arms of Croatia, Dalmatia, Slavonia and the city itself. Its origins reach back to the thirteenth century, blending Gothic and Romanesque work into one of the oldest monuments still standing in the Upper Town.
s: The tiled roof that's Zagreb's calling card
_facts: Parish church of old Zagreb, located in St Mark's Square in the Upper Town (Gradec)
Roof tiles depict the coats of arms of Croatia, Dalmatia, Slavonia and the city of Zagreb
Origins date back to the 13th century
Registered under Cultural Goods of Croatia

n: National and University Library in Zagreb
w: Croatia's written heritage lives inside a cube — a purpose-built modernist block that has housed the national library since 1995. The institution itself dates back to 1607, and its three million items now sit behind a facade about as far from a traditional reading room as it gets.
s: Croatia's national library, inside a cube
_facts: Established in 1607
National library of Croatia and central library of the University of Zagreb
Holds around 3 million items
Located since 1995 in a purpose-built cubical building

w: Built in 1938 as an art gallery, this Ivan Meštrović-designed hall has lived several lives — turned into a mosque under the wartime Independent State of Croatia (locals still call it 'the Mosque'), then recast as the Museum of the Revolution. Returned to Croatian artists in 1990, it's shown exhibitions again since 2006.
s: Art gallery, mosque, then Museum of the Revolution
_facts: Designed by Ivan Meštrović, built 1938 as an art gallery
Converted into a mosque under the Independent State of Croatia (NDH); still colloquially called 'the Mosque'
Became the Museum of the Revolution in post-war Yugoslavia
Returned to the Croatian Association of Artists in 1990; exhibition space again since a 2006 renovation

w: A private collector's haul fills a former gymnasium here — Ante Topić Mimara and his wife Wiltrud amassed everything from Ptolemaic glassware to Qing-dynasty jade, then left paintings by Rubens, Goya, Velázquez and Degas to fill the museum that opened in 1987. At nearly 9,500 square metres, it ranks among the largest art museums anywhere.
s: One collector's haul: Rubens to Qing-dynasty jade
_facts: Opened 17 July 1987, housing the collection of founders Ante Topić Mimara and his wife Wiltrud
Over 3,750 objects across roughly 9,454 square metres
Collection spans Ptolemaic Alexandrian glassware, Qing-dynasty jade and ivory, and paintings by Rubens, Velázquez, Goya, Renoir and Degas
Building originally served as a gymnasium before its 19th-century Beaux-Arts conversion

w: Croatia's government, parliament and constitutional court all cluster around this one square in the Upper Town, alongside the Old City Hall and the deliciously odd Museum of Broken Relationships. St Mark's Church sits at its centre, tiled roof and all — the country's institutional heart packed into one small space.
s: Croatia's government crammed into one square
_facts: Located in the Upper Town (Gradec/Gornji grad)
Home to Banski dvori (Government seat), Sabor Palace (Parliament) and the Constitutional Court
Old City Hall, where Zagreb City Council held its sessions, sits on the corner
Surrounded by museums including the Museum of Broken Relationships and Croatian History Museum
